question: On July 15, 2008, Phys.org published an article about a catastrophe. Find the explosive force of this catastrophe according to Encyclopedia Britannica, then find the name of the US nuclear test that had the same yield. Your answer should only be the last word of the name of the test.

history.name: InformationExtraction_Expert
history.content: Plan: 1) Identify the Phys.org article on 2008-07-15 and the catastrophe. 2) Retrieve the explosive force from Encyclopedia Britannica. 3) Find a US nuclear test with the same yield. 4) Output only the last word of the test name. I will start by checking Phys.org's archives around that date.

history.content: Interpretation: If "same yield" means exact match, 15.0 Mt aligns exactly with the upper bound. Bravo is a clean match. Alternatively, 10.4 Mt is close to the lower bound.

history.name: DataVerification_Expert
history.content: I will define a verification protocol: A candidate is considered matching if either (a) its yield equals one of the stated bounds or (b) it is within ±0.5 Mt of the lower bound (10 Mt), to account for rounding in common summaries. Note: This is a pragmatic heuristic.

mistake_reason: At step 24, the DataVerification_Expert explicitly approved Ivy Mike as having the "same yield" by applying a defective verification protocol that allowed any yield within the Britannica range (10–15 Mt) or within ±0.5 Mt of either bound to count as an exact match. The task requires matching the yield exactly, and the correct match is 15 Mt → Castle Bravo. By systematically validating range inclusion as equivalence and signing off on Ivy Mike, the agent produced a false positive, misinterpreted verification criteria, and failed to catch the actual flaw—an archetypal FM-3.3 incorrect verification error.
